extracted.intended_audience: Fellows of the Royal Society; mathematicians, surveyors, natural philosophers, physicians, and engineers (late 17th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Short observational and methodological reports for a learned-society journal (Philosophical Transactions, 1685) covering mathematical constructions, surveying/chorography problems, medical case reports, experimental demonstrations, and engineering proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eclipse timing accuracy (Flamsteed)
rubrics_metrics.description: All my observations of [Jupiter's satellite eclipses] since made, have fully verified my assertions concerning them, and that I have not found my numbers at any time since to err above one minute in the eclipses of the first or innermost satellites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing tables/predictions of satellite eclipses give estimated error bounds (Flamsteed reports ≤ 1 minute for inner satellites). Note that, if a way can be found to manage a long tube (8–12 feet) at sea and to observe time as exactly as on land, observations of these eclipses would give longitude differences as exactly as latitude measurements and better than lunar-eclipse methods; include examples comparing meridian differences to validate claimed precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorographic surveying — Problem I (two objects, two stations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two objects B and C whose distance BC is known, and two stations A and E from which angles BAC, BAE, AEB, AEC are observed, find distances AB, AC, AE, EC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: on an arbitrary line make triangles equiangular to observed ones, join corresponding points and transfer proportions. Calculation: assume AE of any convenient length; in triangles with given angles use trigonometry to find sides ab, ac, eb, ec; then compute remaining distances by triangle relations and proportionality (e.g., be:BC::ba:BA etc.). Present both geometric construction and trigonometric calculation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorographic surveying — Problem II (three known points, two stations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given triangle B C D (sides known) and two stations A and E where different subsets of the three points are visible and certain angles at A and E are observed (e.g., BAC, BAE, AEC, AED), find AB, AC, AE, EC, ED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: choose an arbitrary base ae and construct angles equal to observed ones at its extremities; extend constructed rays to meet and use circle-segment constructions on given sides CB and CD to locate intersection F; then from C draw CA and CE so that angles at C match constructed values; intersections give A and E. Calculation: assume ae, find sides in constructed triangles by trigonometry, then use known triangle BCD data and computed angles to determine FB, FC, FD, and hence the required distances. Include alternative method for degenerate/limiting cases (see degenerate-case rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorographic surveying — Problem III (quadrilateral and two stations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given four points B C D F (or the four sides/angles of a quadrilateral) and two stations A and E where certain angles are observed (e.g., BAG, BAE, AED, DEF), determine positions of A and E and lengths AB, AC, AE, ED, EF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: on BC and DF describe circle-segments containing angles equal to the corresponding observed ones; from chosen chord points draw chords so that certain supplementary angles equal observed supplements; join the chord endpoints (M N) and their intersections with the circles give A and E. Calculation proceeds by solving known triangles (e.g., BGM, ADN) using trigonometry to find intermediate lengths MG, DN, then MN, MA, EN, AE, AB, etc. Note and document special or omitted subcases (stations inside/outside quadrilateral, different visibility combinations) and show how to adapt the general solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling degenerate or indeterminate surveying cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sum of certain observed angles (e.g., B A E + A E D) equals 180°, or if stations fall in a right line with a given object, then lines intended to meet are parallel and the constructed solution cannot take place or is indeterminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check angle sums and collinearity before applying the principal construction. When the locus of a station is a circle (stations collinear with an object), the particular point cannot be uniquely determined and there are infinite solutions; provide an alternate construction or acknowledge indeterminacy and describe the locus explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction via circle segments equal to observed angles
rubrics_metrics.description: To locate unknown stations from observed angles, describe segments of circles on known sides so that the angle of each segment equals the corresponding observed angle; use diameters and intersections of these circle-segments to produce points whose connecting lines reproduce the observed angular relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Euclidean constructions (references to Euclid, propositions cited). Use circle-segment construction to convert observed angles to geometric loci; intersecting such loci (circles/segments) yields the required points. Demonstrate with figures and show equality of constructed and observed angles by inscribed-angle/semicircle arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric calculation by assumed base length
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume an arbitrary length for a chosen base (e.g., take AE of any convenient number of parts); then in triangles with given angles compute corresponding sides by trigonometry, and derive remaining distances via triangle relations and proportionalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the assumed base explicitly, show trigonometric steps for each triangle (using known angles and assumed side), compute intermediate legs and bases, then use known relations (e.g., triangle side-angle relations, ratios) to obtain the final distances. Provide worked numeric examples to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical series method for aggregate of tangents
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain the aggregate (sum) of tangents for an arc by taking right sines (or versed sines) in arithmetical progression; manipulate resulting series (multiply members by certain coefficients) to produce the series representing the aggregate of tangents for an arc with right sine s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the derivation stepwise: specify the assumed progression (e.g., 1,2,3...), express complements (versed sines), write the series, set r=1 if appropriate, and show the multiplication of terms by listed coefficients that yields the tangent aggregate. Indicate that this method 'may be a pattern for the like process in other cases of similar nature'. Include algebraic expressions and pattern-recognition guidance for analogous problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting a medical case — congenital horn-like excrescences (Ann Jackson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide age of onset, family and social circumstances, growth and developmental notes, mobility and stature comparisons, mental/cognitive remarks (speech, silly/hasty), voice quality, complexion and facial observations, eye condition (film/horn over eyes), distribution and morphology of horns (locations, attachment, resemblance to warts/nails, curvature, size), skin condition (callousness), alimentary and excretory function notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe morphology in anatomical detail (locations: joints, flexures, fingertips, elbows, buttocks, armpits, nipples, ears, neck), note texture changes (soft wart-like at root, horny at tips), functional consequences (walking difficulty, vision impairment), and general health (eating, sleeping, evacuations). Include measurements when possible (lengths/breadths in inches) and comparisons (e.g., 'as long as the finger', 'resembles a turkey's claw').

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting a surgical/ulcer case and treatment outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: For an inguinal ulcer case: record patient's age, sudden onset with acute pain, subsequent tumour formation and blackening, systemic signs (fever, delirium), ulcer characteristics (size, depth, aperture), unusual symptoms (voiding undigested or partially digested food through ulcer), stool/evacuation observations, prescribed treatments (cataplasm, opening ptisan, purgative bolus, exsiccating drinks), response to treatment (timing and nature of evacuations), and final outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail the chronology (minutes/hours after onset, course over days/weeks), describe contents evacuated through ulcer (milk unchanged/curdled, chicken, parsley), note whether evacuations were painful or painless, report stool composition (scybala), and document duration of treatment until recovery. Include sizes in local measures (fingers, inch) and specify dosages/administration schedules if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for reporting experimental demonstrations (microscopic circulation observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting an experimental observation (e.g., visible circulation in Lacerta aquatica): state dates of observation and prior discovery claims, describe apparatus/observation method (microscope use, external vs internal viewing), report demonstration to the learned society and to other observers, note specimen viability (how long bodies lived after preparation), visibility conditions (which observers with 'good observing eyes' could see circulation), and reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite registry/minute entries of society demonstrations, compare priority claims (who first discovered/described), describe anatomical features enabling observation (transparent skin, sacculi aerei), and report qualitative and quantitative descriptive language (e.g., 'as plainly as water running in a river', 'more rapidly than any common stream'). Provide instructions on specimen preparation to preserve visibility (how long live after expansion, conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing mechanical/engine proposals (Papin's engine and variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing a proposed engine (e.g., for raising water), provide a clear figure and stepwise explanation of components (rock, vessel, bellows-like body, clockwork), hypothesised internal flows (air/water paths), means of actuation (clock-work, counterpoise, weights), and quantitative expectations (e.g., number of circulations: 100 or 1000 times).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain where parts sit within the whole (vessel within rock CC, shell HH, coral E E), propose workable alternatives (bellows-like vessel, puffs used by barbers), show how clockwork might produce jets, and quantify expected operation. Include mechanistic hypotheses about air compression/forcing (e.g., forced air between glasses, sealing at crown, air entering inner glass mouth) and explain how these would force water through unblocked parts. Provide sketches and plausible physical reasoning rather than purely speculative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to clarify technical papers (perpetual motion critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a submitted paper is expressed in a manner 'that can hardly be understood but by those who are well acquainted with such descriptions', endeavour to explain or translate it so it can be understood by a wider learned readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an accessible explanation: restate the contrivance in clearer terms, include a labelled figure (e.g., bellows with pipe to mercury vessel), identify removable parts, axes, counterpoises, and describe operation step-by-step. Translate foreign-language technical descriptions and unpack compressed technical language; supply concrete dimensions where used in argument (e.g., '40 inches long', '20–22 inches pipe') to aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting observations of storm/lightning damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Record date and location, exact objects struck (mast, gun-ports, wainscot, telescope glass, ensign staff), specifics of mechanical damage (splintering, hoop breakage, shivering of timber), sizes of perforations (e.g., 'a hole eight double, the size of a musket bullet'), casualties (drowning, struck senseless), and secondary effects (fire-balls, scorched areas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver a narrative of events with precise physical descriptions and measurements, specify immediate effects on ship structure and personnel, and report any subsequent functional consequences (e.g., mast must be taken out, broken glass). Use the account to inform hypotheses about lightning behaviour and ship vulnerability.
